fields.title: The Letter to the Philippians
fields.subtitle: Pros Philippēsious, “To the Philippians”
fields.description: Paul’s warmest letter, written in chains to the first church he founded in Europe, the friends at Philippi who had stood by him from the first day and had just sent him a gift. He does not know whether he will live or die, and finds that either is good: “For me, living is Christ, and dying is gain.” A plea for unity built on the great passage of Christ who emptied himself and took on the form of a servant; Paul counting all his advantages as loss to gain Christ, and running for the prize; two quarrelling friends urged to agree; and joy, prayer, peace and the secret of contentment: “Rejoice in the Lord always.” In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Letter to the Philippians?
qa.answer: The eleventh book of the New Testament, a short letter of the apostle Paul to the church at Philippi in Macedonia, which he had founded around AD 49 (Acts 16). Written from prison, it thanks the Philippians for a gift, tells them his news, urges them to unity and humility after the example of Christ, warns against those who insisted on circumcision, and is full of joy. It contains the great passage on Christ’s humbling and exaltation (2:5–11) and the promise of God’s peace that is beyond all our understanding (4:6–7).

qa.question: Who wrote Philippians, and where was Paul when he wrote it?
qa.answer: The apostle Paul, writing with Timothy (1:1). Almost all scholars agree the letter is his. He was in chains (1:13) and sent greetings from those in the emperor’s household (4:22). The traditional view, still the most widely held, is that he wrote from house arrest in Rome around AD 60–62; some scholars prefer an earlier imprisonment in Ephesus, around AD 54–55, and others Caesarea. Some also think the letter combines two or three shorter notes, though many defend it as a single letter.

qa.question: What does it mean that Christ “emptied himself” in Philippians 2:7?
qa.answer: Paul says that Christ, being in the form of God, did not treat equality with God as something to exploit for himself, but emptied himself by taking on the form of a servant and becoming human, and humbled himself to death on a cross; so God exalted him and gave him the name above every name. The church has always held that the Son did not stop being God. He emptied himself by taking on what he was not, not by giving up what he was. Paul tells the story so that believers will think the same way toward one another (2:5).

qa.question: What does Philippians 4:13 mean by “I can do all things through Christ”?
qa.answer: In this translation the verse reads “I have strength for every situation in the one who makes me strong.” It comes straight after Paul’s words about plenty and hunger: he has learned to be content in every situation, with plenty or with little, and the strength he means is strength to endure both. It is a promise of contentment and endurance whatever comes, more than of success in whatever we attempt. The oldest manuscripts say “the one who makes me strong”; the name “Christ” was added later, though it is plainly Christ whom Paul means.

qa.question: Why is Philippians called the letter of joy?
qa.answer: The words “joy” and “rejoice” run through it more than a dozen times, though Paul is in chains, not knowing whether he will live or die, while some preachers try to make his imprisonment more painful. His joy does not rest on his circumstances: if Christ is proclaimed, he rejoices (1:18). He tells the Philippians, “Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: rejoice!” (4:4), and sets beside it prayer in place of anxiety and the peace of God that guards the heart (4:6–7). It is also a letter between friends, warm with thanks for a partnership that began on the very first day.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
For me, living is Christ, and dying is gain.

— Philippians 1:21

Philippians is a thank-you letter written from a prison. Paul is in chains, waiting to learn whether he will live or die. Some of the preachers around him are trying to make his time in chains more painful. And yet the words “joy” and “rejoice” run through the letter more than a dozen times, and its best-loved verses are about peace, contentment and strength for every situation.

It is also the warmest of Paul’s letters. He writes to the Philippians not as a teacher correcting a wayward church but as a friend writing to friends: “I hold you in my heart.” They had supported him from the very first, and they have just sent him another gift. Philippians is his answer, and it is full of Christ.

The church at Philippi

Philippi stood in the north of Greece, on the great Roman road across Macedonia. It was named after Philip of Macedon, the father of Alexander the Great, and after the civil war battle fought outside it in 42 BC it was resettled with Roman veterans. Acts calls it “a leading city of its district of Macedonia” and “a Roman colony” (Acts 16:12). Its people were proud of their Roman citizenship, a pride Paul draws on when he tells them to “live as citizens in a way worthy of the gospel of Christ” and reminds them that “we hold our citizenship in heaven.”

Paul came there around AD 49, on his second missionary journey, after a vision in the night of a man of Macedonia pleading, “Cross over to Macedonia and help us!” (Acts 16:9). It was the first church he founded in Europe, and Acts tells its beginnings in three unforgettable scenes. A businesswoman named Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth, meets with other women for prayer by a river: “The Lord opened her heart to heed what Paul was saying” (16:14). A slave girl who told fortunes is set free from the spirit that possessed her, and her owners, seeing their profits gone, have Paul and Silas beaten and thrown into prison. And at midnight in the prison, “as Paul and Silas prayed, they sang praises to God, and the prisoners listened” (16:25), until an earthquake shakes the doors open and the jailer and his household believe.

The church that began in Lydia’s house and a jailer’s home never forgot Paul. When he left Macedonia, theirs was the only church that went into partnership with him in giving and receiving, and they sent help to him in Thessalonica more than once (4:15–16).

Where Paul was writing from

Paul is in chains (1:7, 13), and he speaks of “the whole imperial guard” and sends greetings from “those in the emperor’s household” (4:22). The traditional view is that he wrote from Rome, during the two years Acts describes him under guard there, around AD 60–62. Some scholars prefer an earlier imprisonment in Ephesus, around AD 54–55, which would put him closer to Philippi for all the coming and going the letter describes; others suggest Caesarea, where he was held for two years before he was sent to Rome. Imperial guards and imperial servants could be found in all three places. Rome remains the most widely held view.

Some scholars also think the letter as we have it joins together two or three shorter letters, because of the sudden change of tone at 3:2 and because Paul’s thanks for the gift come so late, in 4:10–20. Many others see one letter written by a man whose thoughts and feelings moved quickly, and the book can be read with profit either way.

The shape of the letter

  • Chapter 1: Paul’s chains and the gospel. Thanksgiving and prayer for the Philippians; how his imprisonment has moved the gospel forward; living and dying; and a call to stand firm together.
  • Chapter 2: the mind of Christ. A plea for humility and unity, rooted in the great passage on Christ who emptied himself; and news of Timothy and Epaphroditus.
  • Chapter 3: knowing Christ. A warning against those who insist on circumcision; Paul counts all his advantages as loss; he presses on toward the prize.
  • Chapter 4: joy and peace. Two women urged to agree; rejoicing, prayer and peace; contentment; thanks for the gift; and greetings.

To live is Christ

Paul begins with thanks for their partnership “from the very first day until now”, and with a confidence that rests not on them but on God: “the one who started a good work in you will keep working at it until it is finished on the day of Christ Jesus” (1:6). He prays that their love will overflow, with knowledge and insight to recognize what really matters.

Then he tells them his news, and it is surprisingly good. His chains have moved the gospel forward. Everyone in the guard knows why he is there, and other believers have grown bolder. Some preach Christ out of rivalry, hoping to hurt him. “What does it matter?” If Christ is proclaimed, Paul will rejoice.

He does not know whether he will be released or executed, and he finds that either would be good. “I am pulled in two directions.” To leave this life and be with Christ is far, far better; to stay means fruitful work and their progress in the faith. The sentence that opens this introduction says it all. If life is Christ, then death can only be gain.

The mind of Christ

The church at Philippi was not without its troubles. Two of its leading women, Euodia and Syntyche, were at odds (4:2), and Paul’s plea for unity in chapter 2 may have them in mind. He does not simply tell the Philippians to get along. He shows them Christ:

Among yourselves, think in the way that Christ Jesus also thought, who, being in the form of God, did not treat being equal with God as something to exploit for himself. Rather, he emptied himself, taking on the form of a servant and coming to share the likeness of human beings. And when he was found in outward form as a human being, he humbled himself, becoming obedient all the way to death, death on a cross. That is why God has exalted him far above all and freely given him the name that is above every name, so that every knee will bend before the name of Jesus, in heaven, on earth and below the earth, and every tongue will openly declare that Jesus Christ is Lord, bringing glory to God the Father.

— Philippians 2:5–11

Many readers think these lines were an early Christian hymn, which Paul either quotes or wrote himself. They move like a great V: down from equality with God to the form of a servant, to human likeness, to death, death on a cross; and then up to the highest place, and the name above every name. The last lines take words that God speaks of himself in Isaiah 45:23, every knee bending and every tongue declaring, and apply them to Jesus.

Christians have thought hard about what it means that “he emptied himself.” The church has always held that the Son did not stop being God; he emptied himself by taking on the form of a servant, not by giving up what he was. Paul’s point, though, is practical. This is how the Philippians are to think about one another: not grasping, but giving. “With fear and trembling, keep working out your own salvation,” he goes on, “For it is God who is at work in you.”

Then two examples of that mind at work. Timothy, of whom Paul says, “I have no one else of the same heart.” And Epaphroditus, the Philippians’ own messenger, who brought their gift and fell so sick he almost died, risking his life for the work of Christ.

Everything as loss

Chapter 3 opens with “rejoice in the Lord”, and turns at once into a sharp warning: “Be on guard against the dogs.” Teachers were insisting that Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law to belong to God’s people. Paul answers with his own life. If anyone could boast in human credentials, he could: circumcised on the eighth day, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee, so zealous that he persecuted the church. All of it he now counts as loss, as dung, so that he may gain Christ and be found in him, with the righteousness that comes through faith.

Brothers and sisters, I do not count myself as having taken hold of it. My single aim is this: I put out of mind what is behind me and stretch out for what is in front of me, and I run straight for the goal to win the prize promised by God’s upward call in Christ Jesus.

— Philippians 3:13–14

He has not arrived. He is a runner, straining forward, and he invites them to run with him, waiting for a Saviour from heaven who will change our humble bodies to be like his glorious body.

The peace of God

The last chapter gathers up the whole letter in a few short commands. Stand firm. Agree in the Lord. “Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: rejoice!” Be gentle, because “The Lord is near.” And then one of the most loved passages in the Bible:

Do not worry about anything. Instead, in everything, bring your requests to God through prayer and petition, with thanksgiving. And God’s peace, which is beyond all our understanding, will stand guard over your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.

— Philippians 4:6–7

Only at the end does Paul thank them for their gift, and he does it carefully, almost shyly. He has learned to be content in every situation, with plenty or with little, and he is not after their money. What delights him is what the gift means: a sweet-smelling offering to God, and a sign of a partnership in the gospel. “And my God will fill every need you have.”

How to read Philippians

It is short enough to read in a quarter of an hour. Read it first as what it is, a letter between friends, and imagine it read aloud in Lydia’s house. Then read it slowly.

Notice how often Paul speaks of joy, and where: in chains, in the face of rivals, in the shadow of death. Notice how often he speaks of the mind, of thinking and setting one’s mind. And notice that every part of the letter, its news, its warnings, its thanks, comes back to Christ: living is Christ, thinking as Christ thought, knowing Christ, strength in Christ.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in Philippians are worth knowing about before you begin.

Citizens. In 1:27 the verb Paul uses means to live as a citizen, and the translation keeps that: “live as citizens in a way worthy of the gospel of Christ.” It belongs with 3:20, “we hold our citizenship in heaven”, words that would have rung clearly in a Roman colony.

Christ’s equality with God. In 2:6 the translation reads that he “did not treat being equal with God as something to exploit for himself.” The point is not that he lacked equality with God, but that he did not use it for his own advantage.

“Dung.” In 3:8 Paul uses a deliberately coarse word for what he now thinks of his former advantages, and the translation does not tidy it into “rubbish”.

Philippians 4:13. The familiar “I can do all things through Christ” reads here “I have strength for every situation in the one who makes me strong.” The verse comes straight after Paul’s words about plenty and hunger, and the translation lets it mean what it means there. The oldest manuscripts say “the one who makes me strong”; the name “Christ” was added later, though it is plainly Christ whom Paul means.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Philippians 1
fields.body_html:
Greeting

From Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, to all God’s holy people in Christ Jesus who live in Philippi, together with the overseers and deacons. Grace and peace to you from God our Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ.

Thanks and prayer

Each time I remember you, I give thanks to my God. In every prayer I offer for all of you, I always pray with joy, because from the very first day until now you have been partners with me in the gospel. Of this I am convinced: the one who started a good work in you will keep working at it until it is finished on the day of Christ Jesus. It is only right for me to think this way about all of you, because I hold you in my heart. All of you are partners with me in God’s grace, both in my chains and as I defend the gospel and show that it stands firm. God is my witness how much I long for every one of you with the deep love of Christ Jesus. And this is what I pray: that your love will overflow more and more, with full knowledge and every kind of insight, so that you can test and recognize what really matters. Then on the day of Christ you will be pure and free from stumbling, full of the fruit of righteousness that is produced through Jesus Christ, so that God receives glory and praise.

Paul’s chains move the gospel forward

I want you to understand, brothers and sisters, that what has happened to me has moved the gospel forward rather than holding it back. As a result, the whole imperial guard and everyone else here have come to see that I am in chains for the sake of Christ. And my chains have given most of the brothers and sisters confidence in the Lord, so that they dare to speak the word far more boldly and without fear.

Some, to be sure, are proclaiming Christ from jealousy and a spirit of rivalry; others do it from goodwill. These act out of love, because they know I am stationed here to defend the gospel. The others proclaim Christ out of selfish ambition, with motives that are not pure. They think they can make my time in chains more painful. What does it matter? All that matters is that in every way, whether as a pretext or in truth, Christ is being proclaimed, and in that I rejoice. Yes, and I will go on rejoicing, for I know that through your prayers and the help supplied by the Spirit of Jesus Christ, this will turn out for my salvation. I eagerly expect and hope that I will not be put to shame in anything. Instead, with all boldness, now as always, Christ will be shown to be great in my body, whether through my life or through my death. For me, living is Christ, and dying is gain. But if my life in the body continues, that means fruit from my work. So which would I choose? I cannot say. I am pulled in two directions. My desire is to leave this life and be with Christ, for that is far, far better. But for your sake it is more needful that I stay on in the body. Since I am sure of this, I know that I will stay, and stay on with all of you, to help you move forward and find joy in the faith. Then, when I come back to you, you will have even more reason to boast in Christ Jesus because of me.

Live worthy of the gospel

Just one thing: live as citizens in a way worthy of the gospel of Christ. Then, whether I come and see you or am away and only hear about you, I will know that you are standing firm in one spirit, striving side by side as one for the faith of the gospel, and not letting your opponents frighten you in any way. This courage is a sign to them of their destruction, but of your salvation, and it comes from God. For God has given you the gift, for the sake of Christ, not only of believing in him but also of suffering for him. You are in the same contest that you once watched me face, and that you now hear I am facing still.

fields.title: Philippians 2
fields.body_html:
Think the way Christ thought

So if being in Christ gives you any encouragement, if love brings you any comfort, if you share at all in the Spirit, if you have any tender affection and compassion, then fill my joy to the brim: be of one mind, hold on to the same love, be united in heart, and set your minds on one aim. Do not act out of rivalry or out of a craving for empty glory. Instead, be humble, and regard each other as standing above yourselves. Each of you should care not just about your own concerns but about the concerns of others as well. Among yourselves, think in the way that Christ Jesus also thought, who, being in the form of God, did not treat being equal with God as something to exploit for himself. Rather, he emptied himself, taking on the form of a servant and coming to share the likeness of human beings. And when he was found in outward form as a human being, he humbled himself, becoming obedient all the way to death, death on a cross. That is why God has exalted him far above all and freely given him the name that is above every name, so that every knee will bend before the name of Jesus, in heaven, on earth and below the earth, and every tongue will openly declare that Jesus Christ is Lord, bringing glory to God the Father.

Shine like stars

So then, my beloved, you have always obeyed. Keep at it now, not only as if I were there with you, but much more because I am away: with fear and trembling, keep working out your own salvation. For it is God who is at work in you, producing both the wanting and the doing, for his own good pleasure.

In all you do, avoid complaining and quarreling, so that no one can fault you and you stay pure, God’s children without blemish in the midst of a crooked and distorted generation. Among these people you shine like stars in the world as you keep a firm grip on the word of life. That way, when the day of Christ comes, I can be proud that my running was not wasted and my hard work was not wasted. And even if my life is being poured out like a drink offering over the sacrifice and priestly service that your faith offers, I am glad, and I share my joy with all of you. In the same way, you too should be glad and share your joy with me.

Timothy and Epaphroditus

I hope, in the Lord Jesus, to send Timothy to you before long, so that I too may be heartened when I hear news of you. I have no one else of the same heart, no one who will truly care about your welfare. The others are all pursuing their own concerns, not those of Jesus Christ. But you know how he has proved himself: like a son working alongside his father, he has served with me in spreading the gospel. So he is the one I hope to send, right away, as soon as I see how things will turn out for me. And I am convinced, trusting in the Lord, that I myself will also come before long.

Even so, I have decided I must send Epaphroditus back to you. He is my brother, who has worked beside me and fought beside me, and he is your envoy, whom you sent to serve me in my need. For he has been longing for all of you, and has been deeply upset that you heard he was ill. He really was sick, so sick he almost died. But God showed him mercy, and not only him but me as well, so that I would not have grief on top of grief. That is why I am sending him the more urgently, so that you can see him again and be glad, and I can have less sorrow. So receive him in the Lord with complete joy, and hold people like him in high regard. He came to the edge of death for the work of Christ, staking his life so that he could supply what was missing in your service to me.

fields.title: Philippians 3
fields.body_html:
No confidence in the flesh

Finally, my brothers and sisters, rejoice in the Lord. Writing the same things to you again is no burden to me, and for you it is a safeguard.

Be on guard against the dogs, be on guard against the evil workers, be on guard against the mutilators. For it is we who are the circumcision: we who worship by the Spirit of God, who take pride in Christ Jesus, and who put no confidence in human credentials, even though I myself have grounds for that kind of confidence too.

If anyone else thinks there are grounds for confidence in human credentials, I have more. I was circumcised on the eighth day. I belong to the people of Israel and the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew born of Hebrews. In keeping the law I was a Pharisee; in zeal I persecuted the church; in righteousness as the law defines it, I was beyond reproach.

But whatever was profit to me, I have come to count as loss because of Christ. More than that, I count everything as loss because knowing Christ Jesus my Lord is worth far more than all of it. For his sake I have lost everything, and I count it all as dung, so that I may gain Christ and be found in him, with no righteousness of my own from keeping the law, but with the righteousness that comes through faith in Christ: righteousness from God, resting on faith. I want to know him, to know the power of his resurrection and what it is to share in his sufferings, as I am being shaped into the likeness of his death, hoping that somehow I may arrive at the resurrection from the dead.

Running for the goal

I do not mean that I already have all this, or that I have already been made perfect. But I keep pursuing it, trying to take hold of it, because Christ has taken hold of me. Brothers and sisters, I do not count myself as having taken hold of it. My single aim is this: I put out of mind what is behind me and stretch out for what is in front of me, and I run straight for the goal to win the prize promised by God’s upward call in Christ Jesus. Those of us, then, who are mature should have this mindset. And if your thinking differs at some point, God will reveal that to you as well. In any case, let us keep in step with the point we have already reached.

Brothers and sisters, all of you together, follow my example, and take note of those who live this way, by the pattern you have in us. For many live as enemies of the cross of Christ. I have often told you about them, and now I tell you again, in tears. Destruction is where they will end. The belly is their god, they find their glory in what should make them ashamed, and earthly things fill their minds. But we hold our citizenship in heaven, and it is from there that we are eagerly waiting for a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will change these bodies of our humble state and give them the same form as his glorious body, by the working of his power to bring all things under his rule.

fields.title: Philippians 4
fields.body_html:
Stand firm in the Lord

So then, my dear brothers and sisters, whom I love and long to see, my joy and my crown: stand firm in the Lord in this way, dear friends. I appeal to Euodia and I appeal to Syntyche to agree with each other in the Lord. Yes, and I ask you, my true partner, to help these women. They have fought side by side with me for the gospel, together with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life.

Rejoice in the Lord always

Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: rejoice! Let your gentleness be evident to everyone. The Lord is near. Do not worry about anything. Instead, in everything, bring your requests to God through prayer and petition, with thanksgiving. And God’s peace, which is beyond all our understanding, will stand guard over your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.

Finally, brothers and sisters: all that is true, all that is honorable, all that is just, all that is pure, all that is lovely, all that is well spoken of—if there is any virtue, anything that deserves praise—let your minds dwell on these things. Put into practice what you learned and received from me, what you heard and saw in me. And the God of peace will be with you.

Thanks for their gift

It brought me great joy in the Lord that now at last your care for me has come into bloom again. You had been caring all along; you simply had no chance to show it. I do not say this because I am going short. However things stand with me, I have learned to be content. I know how to get by on little, and I know how to handle having plenty. In each and every situation I have been let into the secret: how to eat my fill and how to go hungry, how to have more than enough and how to do without. I have strength for every situation in the one who makes me strong. All the same, you did a fine thing when you took a share in my hardship.

You know it yourselves, Philippians: in those first days of the gospel, when I left Macedonia, yours was the only church that went into partnership with me in an account of giving and receiving. Even in Thessalonica you sent help for my needs more than once. It is not the gift I am after. What I am after is the profit that keeps adding up in your account. Everything has been paid to me in full, and I have more than enough. Since Epaphroditus brought me what you sent, I have all I need. Your gift is a sweet-smelling offering, a sacrifice God accepts, one that pleases him. And my God will fill every need you have, in keeping with his glorious wealth in Christ Jesus. Glory be to our God and Father for ever and ever. Amen.

Final greetings

Greet every one of God’s holy people in Christ Jesus. The brothers and sisters who are with me send you greetings. All God’s holy people here greet you, especially those in the emperor’s household. May the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
And my God will fill every need you have, in keeping with his glorious wealth in Christ Jesus. Glory be to our God and Father for ever and ever. Amen.

— Philippians 4:19–20

Philippians ends with a promise and a doxology. The church had met Paul’s need, and now Paul, who has nothing to give them in return, hands them over to a God who has everything. It is how the whole letter works. A prisoner with no certain future writes to a small church with troubles of its own, and almost every sentence turns toward Christ, until the letter closes in glory to God the Father, for ever and ever.

The question the letter leaves

“For me, living is Christ.” Paul says it as plainly as anyone could, and the sentence waits for each reader to finish it in their own way. For me, living is my work, my family, my comfort, my reputation? Paul had his list too, and he counted it all as loss. He was not despising the good things of life; he was saying that none of them could carry the weight of being his life.

The letter does not leave that as an idea. It turns it into a way of treating other people. If Christ, who was in the form of God, emptied himself and took on the form of a servant, then the people who belong to him will regard each other as standing above themselves, and care about the concerns of others. Euodia and Syntyche are asked to agree in the Lord, and the whole church is asked to help them. Joy, in Philippians, is not a mood. It is what grows in people who have stopped grasping.

Where the letter points

It points forward. Paul is waiting for a Saviour from heaven, for the day of Christ, for the resurrection from the dead. The God who started a good work in the Philippians will keep working at it until it is finished. Nothing in the letter is meant to be the last word: not Paul’s chains, not the rivals preaching Christ to spite him, not the quarrel in the church, not even death.

We do not know for certain how Paul’s imprisonment ended. Christian tradition says that he was released for a time and later put to death in Rome under Nero. But the church at Philippi went on. Some fifty years later, the Philippians wrote to Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, and his reply survives. He reminds them that Paul “wrote you a letter, which, if you carefully study, you will find to be the means of building you up” in the faith.

Where to go from here

Polycarp’s advice still holds, and many of the church’s best teachers have helped readers study this letter. A few places to begin, all in this library:

  • The church at Philippi. The Epistle and Martyrdom of Polycarp, his letter to the Philippians, with the story of his death; and Devoted to Prayer, whose chapters “The Place of Prayer by the River” and “Songs at Midnight” tell how the church began (Acts 16).
  • On the mind of Christ (chapter 2). Andrew Murray’s Humility, especially “The Secret of Redemption” (2:5–8) and “Humility and Death to Self” (2:8); Athanasius’s Against the Arians, whose first Discourse explains 2:9–10; and John Chrysostom’s sermon Concerning Lowliness of Mind, on 1:18.
  • On working out your salvation (2:12–13). Martyn Lloyd-Jones’s Working Out Our Own Salvation, and John Wesley’s On Working out our own Salvation, in his Sermons on Several Occasions.
  • On knowing Christ (chapter 3). George Whitefield’s The Power of Christ’s Resurrection (3:10), in Selected Sermons of George Whitefield.
  • On joy, prayer and contentment (chapter 4). Alexander Maclaren’s Rejoice Evermore (4:4) and How to Say ‘Thank You’ (4:10–14); Charles H. Spurgeon’s “Prayer, the Cure for Care” (4:6), in Mighty Power in Prayer; and Thomas Watson’s The Art of Divine Contentment, a whole book on 4:11.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Philippians in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this letter.

But the best next step may be to read Philippians again, slowly, and to take its fourth chapter at its word. Bring your requests to God, with thanksgiving, and then turn your mind where Paul turns it:

Finally, brothers and sisters: all that is true, all that is honorable, all that is just, all that is pure, all that is lovely, all that is well spoken of—if there is any virtue, anything that deserves praise—let your minds dwell on these things.

— Philippians 4:8
